title: Spermidine Associated with Gut Microbiota Protects Against MRSA Bloodstream Infection by Promoting Macrophage M2 Polarization

sections.abstract:
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a major human pathogen that causes various diseases. Extensive researches highlight the significant role of gut microbiota and its metabolites, particularly spermidine, in infectious diseases. However, the immunomodulatory mechanisms of spermidine in MRSA-induced bloodstream infection remain unclear. Here, we confirmed the protective effects of spermidine in bloodstream infection in mice. Spermidine reduced the bacterial load and expression of inflammatory factors by shifting the macrophage phenotype to an anti-inflammatory phenotype, ultimately prolonging the survival of the infected mice. The protective effect against MRSA infection may rely on the elevated expression of protein tyrosine phosphatase nonreceptor 2 (PTPN2). Collectively, these findings confirm the immunoprotective effects of spermidine via binding to PTPN2 in MRSA bloodstream infection, providing new ideas for the treatment of related infectious diseases.

Keywords: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, bloodstream infection, gut microbiota, spermidine, macrophages, PTPN2
sections.methods:
Ampicillin, neomycin, metronidazole, vancomycin, and spermidine were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich; animal experiments were conducted using 6-week-old female BALB/c mice; All mice were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of Anhui Province (Hefei, China). The mice were kept under a 12-hour light/dark cycle with controlled humidity and temperature and were provided with food and water ad libitum for 3 days.

Mice received antibiotic treatment via drinking water for 21 days. The antibiotic cocktail included ampicillin (1.0 g/L), neomycin (1.0 g/L), metronidazole (1.0 g/L), and vancomycin (0.5 g/L), as previously described. Antibiotic treatment was stopped 5 days prior to infection. According to laws of drug metabolism, the drug usually resolved its effects after 5 half-lives.The half-life of ampicillin was 1.5 h, that of neomycin was 4 h, that of metronidazole was 8 h, and that of vancomycin was 6 h, so stopping for 5 days was enough to remove the effect of antibiotics. Mice received 3 mmol of spermidine in their drinking water for 2 weeks.

Fresh feces from randomly chosen healthy BALB/c mice were collected daily at approximately. Next, 0.5 g of feces was vortexed for 5 min in 5 mL of PBS followed by 5 min standing to precipitate particles. Subsequently, mice were given 500 μL/day of the fecal solution by oral gavage for 5 days before to MRSA infection and after antibiotic water was stopped.

Staphylococcus aureus strains USA300 were cultured overnight at 37 °C in tryptic soy broth. For infection, the overnight culture was subcultured until it reached the exponential phase (OD600 = 1.0). The bacteria were then diluted to different concentrations for the animal model. For bloodstream infection model, mice were intravenously challenged with S. aureus USA300 (2.5 × 10 7 CFU/mouse) and were euthanized 24h postinfection, at which point the blood, lungs, livers, and kidneys were collected for the subsequent experiments. To assess bacterial load, livers and kidneys were weighed, then homogenized in 1 mL ice-cold phosphate buffered saline (PBS) for 5 min at 60 Hz and 4 °C. Tissue homogenates and blood samples were diluted in 1 mL of PBS and plated on TSA plates. Plates were incubated overnight at 37 °C for 18 h under aerobic conditions and bacterial colonies were counted. The CFU/mL of blood and CFU/g of tissue were calculated. For histological examination, the lungs, livers, and kidneys were dissected from mice, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 h, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 4 μm, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. For survival experiment, BALB/c mice were intravenously inoculated with 100 μL of S. aureus USA300 suspension at a concentration of 5 × 10 8 CFU mL –1 . Survival was monitored over 3 days.

Mouse sera and cell culture supernatants were collected and stored at −80 °C. Inflammatory cytokine concentrations (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-10, IL-1β) were measured using BOSTER ELISA kits (China) following the manufacturer’s instructions: prior to use, all reagents were allowed to reach room temperature. Subsequently, 100 μL of both the sample and the standard were dispensed into each well. The samples were incubated at 37 °C for 1.5 h. Following this, the samples and standards were carefully removed, and biotinylated antibody was introduced into each well, followed by another incubation period of 1 h under the same temperature conditions. The wells were rinsed with a wash solution on three occasions before the addition of the ABC antibody, after which the samples were incubated for an additional 30 min at 37 °C. The samples were washed five additional times. 90 μL of TMB was added to each well and incubated for 15 min at 37 °C. The reaction was stopped by adding a stop solution, thoroughly mixed, and immediately read at 450 nm using a plate reader.

Stool bacterial DNA was extracted using a QIAamp DNA Stool Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA samples were diluted in sterile water to achieve a concentration of 1 ng/μL. Using certain primers, the 16S rRNA genes of four different regions (16SV3–V4) were amplified. The Illumina 16S Metagenomic Sequencing Library preparation guide was utilized for 16S rRNA gene amplification, transcription, labeling, and hybridization. All libraries were sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq PE250 platform (San Diego, CA, USA) at PANOMIX Biomedical Tech. Co., Ltd. (Suzhou, China).

Targeted metabolomics analysis of polyamine in feces and serum was conducted at Shanghai Biotree Biotech Co., Ltd. Specimens were blended at 35 Hz for 4 min and sonicated in an ice–water bath for 5 min, repeated 3 times. Subsequently, the samples underwent a derivatization process with minor adjustments. An 80 μL aliquot of the supernatant was transferred to an autosampler vial for UHPLC-MS/MS analysis.The analysis utilized an Agilent 6460 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer. The calibration standard solution was serially diluted by a factor of 2. The standard solutions underwent UHPLC-MRM-MS analysis.

After euthanasia, the leg muscles and cartilage of mice were fully removed, and bone marrow was finally exposed. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) were produced by extracting bone marrow from the femur and tibia, followed by culturing the cells in DMEM with 10% FBS, 100 IU/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 25 ng/mL macrophage-colony stimulating factor (M-CSF). Cultures were kept at 37 °C in 5% CO 2 , with the medium refreshed every 2–3 days.

A suspension of BMDMs was seeded in 24-well plates containing DMEM medium with either PBS or 20 μM spermidine for 12 h, followed by a 45 min incubation with S. aureus (MOI = 30:1) at 37 °C. Then, the cells were washed two times with PBS containing 10 μg/mL lysostaphin. After adding fresh DMEM supplemented with 10 μg/mL lysostaphin and 8 μg/mL vancomycin, the cells were cultured for 60 min in order to eliminate any extracellular bacteria. After two rounds of cold PBS containing lysostaphin washing, macrophages were lysed to ascertain the amount of internalized bacteria ( t = 0 h, phagocytosis) in PBS with 1% Triton X-100 added. To evaluate bacterial killing, more cells were cultured for an additional 3 h.

Total RNA from the cells was isolated using the TRIzol reagent (Takara, Japan) in accordance with the provided protocol. cDNA was synthesized using a cDNA synthesis kit (Takara, Japan) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For mRNA detection, GAPDH served as an internal control. Real-time PCR was conducted using SYBR Green (TaKaRa, Japan) with a three-step real-time PCR system (Light Cycler 96, Roche). Primer sequences are provided in Table S1.

Total protein from the cell lysate was isolated using SDS-PAGE and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes. Membranes were blocked for 1.5 h at room temperature using 5% nonfat milk that had been diluted with TBS-T. Membranes were treated three times with TBS-T after being incubated with the corresponding primary antibodies for an overnight period at 4 °C. Following a 1 h incubation period at room temperature, the secondary antibody was cleaned three times with TBS-T. The ECL Plus Western blotting detection system was utilized to identify the membranes. Furthermore, the amounts of β-tubulin protein functioned as an internal control. Antibodies specific for Arg1 and iNOS (1:1000, Abcam, USA), T-STAT1, p-STAT1, and PTPN2 (1:1000, CST, USA), and β-tubulin (1:1000, Affinity, USA) were used.

Flow cytometry was carried out in this manner: Briefly, 500 μL of cold 5 mM EDTA in PBS was added to each well, and the cells were incubated at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 for at least 5 min. Cells were collected and incubated with anti-CD16/32 at 4 °C for 30 min. Following the manufacturer’s guidelines, the cell suspension was incubated for 20 min with anti-F4/80 FITC, anti-CD11b BV 510, anti-Arg1 PE, and anti-iNOS APC antibodies (Biolegend, USA).For on-machine analysis, the cells were resuspended in 300 μL of PBS after three ice-cold PBS rinses.

Date are derived from at least three independent experiments. The mean ± SEM is used to express the results. Unpaired student’s t tests were used for two-group comparisons, while one-way or two-way ANOVA was employed for multiple group analyses. p values below 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All graphs were generated using Adobe Illustrator 2021 or Graph Pad Prism 9.
sections.results:
A mouse bloodstream infection model was developed to investigate the relationship between MRSA infection and gut microbiota. Mouse feces were analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing 24 h postinfection and compared to the samples from healthy mice. The OTUs with classification information annotations were used to compare the two groups. Post-MRSA infection, the Venn diagram revealed 1630 unique OTUs in MRSA-infected mice, 2578 unique OTUs in the control group, and 885 shared OTUs between both groups ( Figure 1 A). Although the Chao1 and Shannon indices showed no significant differences ( Figure 1 B), principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed distinct clustering between samples from MRSA-infected individuals and healthy controls ( Figure 1 C). This suggests that MRSA infection significantly alters the composition of intestinal flora in mice without affecting its overall abundance compared with the control group. At the phylum level, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, and Proteobacteria were dominant in both groups. Proteobacteria levels remained unchanged among the two groups. However, compared with the healthy control group, MRSA-infected mice exhibited significantly reduced Firmicutes levels and increased abundances of Bacteroidetes and Verrucoides ( Figure 1 D). These results suggested that MRSA-induced BSI led to changes in the intestinal flora of mice. We subsequently conducted functional prediction of infected mouse gut microbiota using PICRUSt2. The infection group exhibited altered abundance in metabolic pathways related to substance generation compared to the control group, with notable changes in the production of amines and polyamines ( Figure 1 E). However, the role of the disorganized gut flora in bloodstream infection is unclear.

Bloodstream infection caused by MRSA altered gut microbiota in mice. (A) Venn diagram of OTUs. (B, C) Analysis of alpha diversity and beta diversity of gut microbiota in bloodstream infection and healthy mice. (D) Relative abundance of gut microbiota at the phylum level. (E) The MetaCyc pathway predicted by PICRUSt2. CON, PBS treatment group. SA, MRSA infection group. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant. Data were presented as the mean ± SEM.

To assess the influence of gut microbiota on MRSA-induced bloodstream infection, mice were administered a mixture of antibiotics (ABX) to disrupt the gut microbiota ( Figure S1A ). Mice from both the untreated and gut microbiota-dysbiosis groups were infected with MRSA. By 96 h after inoculation, all ABX mice succumbed to MRSA infection, whereas half of the control mice survived ( Figure 2 A). During MRSA-induced bloodstream infection, ABX mice exhibited higher bacterial loads in blood, kidney, and liver tissues compared to the untreated group ( Figure 2 B). Compared to healthy mice, bloodstream infection caused lung damage and the migration of MRSA from the blood to the kidney caused multiple abscesses. HE staining showed that ABX treatment caused further aggravated lung damage and increased the number of renal abscesses in infected mice ( Figure 2 C,D). The ABX group exhibited significantly higher levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 compared to those of the infection group ( Figure 2 E). These results indicated that intestinal microflora depletion can significantly aggravate bloodstream infection caused by MRSA in mice, which is manifested by impaired bacterial clearance and excessive inflammatory response.

Dysbiosis of gut microbe exacerbates bloodstream infection. (A) The survival rate of MRSA-induced bloodstream infection in different groups ( n = 8). (B) The bacterial load in the circulation and visceral organs in different groups ( n = 6). (C) HE staining of lung and kidney in different groups. (D) Inflammation scores of lung and counts of renal abscess in different groups ( n = 6). (E) The level of pro-inflammatory factors in different groups ( n = 6). Data are representative results from three independent experiments with at least n = 6 mice per group, each. Dots represent individual mice, asterisks denote statistical differences (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant). Vehicle, ddH 2 O treatment and infection group. ABX, antibiotics treatment and infection group. ABX + FMT, antibiotics and fecal microbiota transplantation treatment and infection group.

To verify whether fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) rescued the effects of gut microbiota depletion, an FMT model was established using fecal gavage. FMT reversed the ABX-induced increase in mouse mortality ( Figure 2 A). Compared with the ABX-treated group, a lower bacterial load in the blood, liver, and kidney tissues was observed in the ABX + FMT group ( Figure 2 B). The ABX + FMT group had a lower pathological score for the lung tissue and fewer renal abscesses ( Figure 2 C,D). FMT also reduced the levels of pro-inflammatory factors ( Figure 2 E). These results indicated that intestinal flora play a protective role during MRSA-induced bloodstream infection.

The gut microbiota affects the host’s physiopathological state by generating small-molecule metabolites that enter the bloodstream and alter the immune environment of extraintestinal organs. 8 To elucidate the metabolomic profiles of MRSA-infected mice, we conducted comprehensive untargeted serum metabolomic sequencing via liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. Using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database, differences in metabolite abundance between MRSA-infected and healthy groups were identified ( Figure 3 A). The impact of MRSA-induced bloodstream infection on serum metabolic pathways was examined, revealing changes in arginine metabolic pathways through enrichment analysis ( Figure 3 B), consistent with alterations observed in mouse feces metabolites ( Figure S2A,B ). Arginine metabolism-related derivatives encompass compounds like creatine, urea, and polyamines ( Figure 3 C), with prior research indicating that polyamines can be synthesized by the gut microbiota. 21 Therefore, to clarify the specific changes in polyamines in serum of mice with MRSA-induced bloodstream infection, we performed targeted metabolomics sequencing of mouse serum. After MRSA infection, the concentration of spermidine in serum and feces decreased significantly ( Figure 3 D), consistent with the same changes in ABX mice ( Figure S3 ). To explore the correlation between gut microbiota and metabolites during MRSA infection, we performed a Spearman’s correlation analysis between metabolites and bacterial taxa at the genus level. There were statistically significant interactions between the 3 metabolites and 29 bacterial taxa ( Figure S2C ). To further clarify that spermidine was derived from the gut microbiota, we examined the spermidine levels in the feces and serum of mice after FMT treatment. FMT treatment increased spermidine levels in feces and serum compared to the ABX group, indicating that these changes likely originated from the gut microbiota ( Figure 3 E). Nevertheless, the regulatory relationship between gut microbiota-derived polyamine metabolites and bloodstream infection caused by MRSA is unclear.

Bloodstream infection caused by MRSA alters serum metabolites in mice. (A) Volcano plot of serum metabolites. Red and blue circles indicate the significantly increased and decreased expression, respectively. (B) Significant differential metabolites of KEGG pathway enrichment. Arginine metabolism are highlighted in red. (C) Arginine metabolism-related derivatives. (D) The concentration of polyamines in serum and feces from MRSA-infected and healthy mice. (E) The concentration of spermidine in serum and feces from ABX, ABX + FMT, and healthy mice. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant. Data were presented as the mean ± SEM.

To further evaluate whether spermidine could ameliorate bloodstream infection, mice were administered water containing 3 mmol/L spermidine for 2 weeks, and after supplementation, the serum spermidine level increased from 569.9 to 1183.5 nmol/L ( Figure 4 A). Surprisingly, at a lethal dose of MRSA, spermidine supplementation significantly increased the survival rate ( Figure 4 B). Next, we assessed the impact of spermidine on bacterial clearance and the systemic inflammatory response. Preinfection administration of spermidine significantly reduced bacterial counts in the circulation, liver, and kidney, suggesting enhanced bacterial clearance ( Figure 4 C). Spermidine treatment significantly decreased the expression of TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β compared with the infection group ( Figure 4 D), indicating a reduction in systemic inflammation.

Spermidine derived from gut microbiota relieves MRSA infection. (A) The level of spermidine in serum of mice with or without spermidine treatment. (B) Survival rates of MRSA infection in SPD and PBS treatment group ( n = 8). (C) Bacterial load in the circulation and visceral organs in SPD and PBS treatment group ( n = 6). (D) Levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 in different groups. (E) HE staining of lung tissue and kidney tissue in different groups. (F) Inflammation scores of lung and counts of renal abscess in different groups. (G) Organ dysfunction biomarker in different groups. (H) Gut permeability in different groups. Data are representative results from three independent experiments with at least n = 6 mice per group, each. Dots represent individual mice, asterisks denote statistical differences (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant). CON, no treatment group. PBS, PBS treatment and infection group. SPD, spermidine treatment and infection group.

We further assessed the effect of spermidine on organ damage and gut permeability after MRSA infection challenge. HE staining showed that spermidine supplementation significantly alleviated pathological damage in the lung and reduced the number of renal abscesses ( Figure 4 E,F). We selected serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) to indicate general cell injury, alanine transaminotransferase (ALT) for liver injury, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) for kidney injury. Spermidine administration reduced serum LDH, ALT, and BUN levels induced by MRSA infection, suggesting decreased tissue and organ damage ( Figure 4 G). Then, FITC-dextran was used to investigate whether spermidine could reduce intestinal permeability The results showed that early administration of spermidine reduced the increase in intestinal permeability caused by MRSA infection ( Figure 4 H). Our findings suggested that spermidine may influence the innate immune response to MRSA infection. However, the precise regulatory mechanisms require further investigation.

To assess SPD’s protective role against bloodstream infection, we examined its impact on bacterial growth. The results showed no significant difference in bacterial growth between SPD-treated and untreated groups ( Figure S4A ), indicating that SPD may regulate the host immune response to protect against MRSA infection. Previous researches indicated that SPD regulated macrophage functions, influencing IBD and tumors. 22 , 23 To clarify whether the protective effect of SPD against BSI caused by MRSA was generated through macrophages, we first performed in vitro experiments. Although SPD did not enhance the phagocytosis of MRSA by BMDMs ( Figure 5 A), it could promote the ability of macrophages to kill bacteria, and the number of CFU confirmed this ( Figure 5 B).

SPD protects against MRSA infection through macrophages. (A-,B) Phagocytosis and bacterial killing by BMDMs in the presence or absence of SPD. (C-,D) The survival rate of MRSA-induced bloodstream infection and the level of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 in macrophage-depleted mice with or without SPD treatment. (E-,F) HE staining of lung tissue and inflammation scores of lung in macrophage-depleted mice with or without SPD treatment. (G-,H) The bacterial load in the circulation and visceral organs and organs dysfunction biomarker with or without SPD treatment in macrophage-depleted or control mice. Data are representative results from three independent experiments with at least n = 6 mice per group, each. Dots represent individual mice, asterisks denote statistical differences (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant). CL, clodronate liposomes. EL, empty liposomes.

Next, we further investigated the role of macrophages in SPD-mediated protection in vivo. Then mouse macrophages were depleted using clodronate liposomes. After macrophage depletion, SPD supplementation did not improve the survival of infected mice ( Figure 5 C). Meanwhile, SPD administration did not reduce the concentration of inflammatory factors in the serum ( Figure 5 D). HE staining showed that SPD pretreatment also failed to alleviate pathological lung injury ( Figure 5 E,F). The bacterial load in the circulation, liver, and kidney did not decrease, and serum LDH, ALT, and BUN did not change after pretreatment with clodronate liposomes ( Figure 5 G,H), indicating that bacterial clearance ability and organ-protective effect produced by SPD in bloodstream infection were significantly impaired. The results indicated that macrophages may play a role in the protective effects of SPD against MRSA bloodstream infection.

Previous studies indicated that spermidine regulated macrophage polarization to inhibit inflammatory responses in inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. 22 , 24 Therefore, we hypothesized that SPD may also play a protective role in MRSA bloodstream infection by promoting macrophage anti-inflammatory (M2)-like polarization. Markers of pro-inflammatory (M1) and anti-inflammatory (M2) macrophage phenotypes were examined in BMDMs and mouse mononuclear macrophage cells following SPD treatment. RT-PCR and WB results indicated a decrease in RNA and protein levels of Arg1 in BMDMs after MRSA infection, while iNOS levels significantly increased. SPD treatment increased Arg1 expression and decreased iNOS expression in infected cells ( Figure 6 A). The alterations in Arg1 and iNOS were consistent in RAW 264.7 cells ( Figure 6 B). Thereafter, LPS and IFN-γ were used to create a transition to M1 phenotype, while a transition to M2 phenotype was created using IL4 in BMDMs. Flow cytometry analysis indicated that SPD treatment significantly elevated the frequency of iNOS – Arg1 + M2 macrophages while decreasing the frequency of iNOS + Arg1 – M1 macrophages ( Figure 6 C,D). Post-SPD treatment, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 concentrations significantly decreased, while IL-10 levels increased in both BMDMs and RAW 264.7 cells infected with MRSA ( Figure 6 E). The results indicated that SPD administration promoted a notable shift from M1 to M2 phenotype in MRSA-infected macrophages.

SPD drives M2 polarization of macrophages. (A) The RNA and protein levels of iNOS and Arg1 in BMDMs with or without SPD treatment. (B) The RNA and protein levels of iNOS and Arg1 in RAW 264.7 cells with or without SPD treatment. (C, D) The expression of Arg1 and iNOS in BMDMs with or without SPD treatment via flow cytometry analysis. (E) The RNA and protein levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-10, and IL-6 in BMDMs and RAW 264.7 cells with or without SPD treatment. CON, no treatment group. PBS, PBS treatment and infection group. Data are representative results from three independent experiments. Asterisks denote statistical differences (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant). SPD, spermidine treatment and infection group.

Previous studies indicated that SPD regulated diseases progression by enhancing PTPN2 expression in various cells. 25 To clarify whether SPD may affect the expression of PTPN2 in macrophages during MRSA infection, we analyzed the effect of SPD on PTPN2 activity in BMDMs and RAW 264.7 cells. MRSA infection elevated both PTPN2 mRNA expression and the relative level of PTPN2 protein compared to the control group. The SPD treatment allowed for further activation of PTPN2 in infected BMDMs ( Figure 7 A–C). The changes of PTPN2 in SPD-treated RAW 264.7 cells were consistent with those observed in BMDMs ( Figure 7 D–F). As a tyrosine phosphatase, PTPN2 can interact with various substrates and negatively regulate the STAT1 phosphorylation, thereby regulating the polarization of macrophages. Therefore, the phosphorylation level of STAT1 were examined in macrophages. The results showed that STAT1 phosphorylation was enhanced in both infected BMDMs and RAW 264.7 cells, whereas it was decreased after SPD pretreatment. We constructed PTPN2 knockdown RAW 264.7 cells to further verify that SPD-regulated PTPN2 promoted the transition of the macrophage polarization phenotype. The knockdown efficiency of the sh-RNA sequences was assessed using RT-PCR ( Figure S4B ). SPD pretreatment did not suppress IL-1β and TNF-α expression in PTPN2 knockdown RAW 264.7 cells. Consistent with this finding, SPD treatment failed to promote Arg1 expression, whereas its inhibitory effect on iNOS was abrogated ( Figure 7 G). These results indicated that down-regulation of PTPN2 expression prevented the regulation of SPD for the polarized phenotypic transition in macrophages.

SPD controls M2 macrophages differentiation via PTPN2 activation. (A) The RNA levels of PTPN2 in BMDMs with or without SPD treatment. (B–,C) The protein levels of PTPN2 and p-STAT1 in BMDMs with or without SPD treatment. (D) The RNA levels of PTPN2 in RAW 264.7 cells with or without SPD treatment. (E-,F) The protein levels of PTPN2 and p-STAT1 in RAW 264.7 cells with or without SPD treatment. (G) The RNA levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, Arg1, and iNOS with or without SPD treatment in PTPN2 knockdown or normal control cells. Data are representative results from three independent experiments. Asterisks denote statistical differences (* p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001, **** p < 0.0001, ns: not significant).
sections.discussion:
MRSA can cause various infections by accumulating in the skin, soft tissues, lungs, bloodstream, bones, and joints. 26 Bloodstream infection caused by MRSA significantly impacted morbidity and mortality in hospitalized patients and were the leading cause of coinfection and superinfection during the COVID-19 epidemic. 27 Increasing studies of gut microbiota modulating host immune function have provided novel strategies for the treatment of infectious diseases. 28 In this study, spermidine was shown to be a key metabolite associated with gut microbiota, which alleviated bloodstream infection caused by MRSA. After infection with MRSA or depletion of the intestinal microbiota, the spermidine levels in serum and feces decreased significantly. Pretreatment with SPD enhanced survival, decreased bacterial load, and reduced inflammation in mice. In addition, SPD treatment induced macrophages polarization toward the M2 phenotype by enhancing PTPN2 expression to inhibited STAT1 activation.

In recent decades, various diseases have been linked to gut microbiota dysbiosis. 29 Infectious diseases caused a reduction in Firmicutes and an increase in Proteobacteria or Bacteroidetes in the gut microbiota, aligning with the changes observed in MRSA bloodstream infection. 30 − 32 The gut microbiota generate various metabolites, such as SCFAs, secondary bile acids, and tryptophan derivatives, which enter the bloodstream to modulate systemic immunity and have been studied across multiple diseases. However, studies of polyamine metabolites produced by intestinal flora are still rare. We analyzed polyamine levels in both stool and serum samples from mice. The study found altered polyamine metabolites in stool and serum of MRSA-infected mice, with decreased serum levels of putrescine and spermidine. However, it is of interest that spermine, which is a further metabolite of spermidine, did not exhibit any changes in stool and serum. As for the phenomenon of no difference in spermine observed in this study, we are currently unable to provide an explanation. More comprehensive metabolic studies may be necessary to uncover the mechanism behind this phenomenon. Spearman’s analysis showed that polyamine metabolites in serum after infection were associated with intestinal flora, whereas Clostridium and Lactobacillus were associated with intestinal SPD production. 21 , 33 Importantly, FMT treatment increased the concentration of spermidine in serum and feces, which confirmed that spermidine was associated with intestine flora. Spermidine levels in organisms are closely associated with gut microbiota and can be readily detected in the intestinal lumen, even during fasting. Through the detection of intestinal polyamine concentration of germ-free mice before and after colonization, most of spermidine in the colon cavity of mice was produced by intestinal flora. 34 Seventy-four gut bacteria associated with spermidine metabolism were identified from the human gut, demonstrating that, like mice, the species and abundance of human gut flora are related to spermidine levels. 35

Spermidine, a naturally occurring polyamine present in all living organisms, is also produced by gut microbes. SPD exhibits a range of beneficial effects, including anti-inflammatory action, antioxidant activity, and the promotion of mitochondrial metabolism and respiration; thus, SPD plays a protective role in several diseases. 36 Initially, SPD induced autophagy and prolonged lifespan. 37 Subsequent studies indicated that spermidine’s effects were linked to autophagy stimulation. Knocking down ornithine decarboxylase, the key enzyme in spermidine synthesis, reduced spermidine levels and inhibited autophagy; 38 however, some evidence suggested that spermidine may activate Nrf2 to provide protective effects independently of the autophagy pathway. 39 , 40 Spermidine was also able to regulate the cellular immune metabolism. Blocking polyamine biosynthesis, or inducing spermidine catabolism, damaged tricarboxylic acid cycle in murine embryonic fibroblasts and bone-marrow-derived macrophages, which exerting an impact on cellular function. 41 Recent studies indicated that SPD inhibited NOD-like receptor protein-3 inflammasome activation in macrophages and alleviated acute kidney injury in mice. 42 SPD treatment enhanced mitochondrial metabolism in CD8+ T cells, thereby boosting the effectiveness of PD-1 immunosuppressive therapy. 43 However, the role of SPD in infectious diseases, especially in bloodstream infection caused by MRSA, is unknown. Therefore, mice were orally supplemented with 3 mM spermidine, and the concentration of spermidine in serum was elevated compared to control mice, indicating that the administration of 3 mM of spermidine can generate concentrations that exceed physiological relevance. Given the protective role of SPD in MRSA bloodstream infection, we focused on measuring serum spermidine levelsl. This study is the first to demonstrate that intestinal microbiota-associated SPD decreases susceptibility to MRSA infection, as indicated by a lower bacterial burden and enhanced survival. Putrescine levels in serum also decreased following MRSA infection or ABX treatment, but supplementation with putrescine did not enhance the survival rate of MRSA-infected mice ( Figure S5 ).

Professional phagocytes, particularly macrophages, are critical innate immune cells that interact with S. aureus as gatekeepers to control and resolve infection. 44 , 45 SPD administration promoted bacterial killing by macrophages in vitro. SPD supplementation did not improve survival and resulted in the loss of the ability to clear tissue bacteria in macrophage-depleted mice, suggesting that SPD exerted a protective effect against MRSA infection by regulating macrophages function. Macrophages are highly plastic and their phenotypic transition from anti-inflammatory (M2)-like to pro-inflammatory (M1)-like can modulate the host immune response. 46 MRSA infection resulted in a change of the macrophage phenotype to M1-like, increased the level of pro-inflammatory factors and decreased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines. 47 SPD treatment elevated Arg1 expression, decreased TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β levels, and upregulated IL-10 level. These results indicated that SPD may decrease tissues bacterial load by promoting bacterial clearance effect of macrophages and alleviate inflammatory response by promoting the conversion to the M2 phenotype. STAT1 phosphorylation can regulate polarization phenotype of macrophages. 48 Therefore, we confirmed that STAT1 phosphorylation in macrophages decreased after SPD treatment, thus skewing macrophages toward the M2 phenotype.

However, the specific mechanism through SPD that negatively regulates STAT1 phosphorylation during MRSA infection remains unclear. PTPN2, a widely expressed nonreceptor tyrosine phosphatase, serves as a crucial negative regulator of various cytokine signaling pathways. 49 The development of immune cells in PTPN2 knockout mice was impeded, leading to the overproduction of cytokines and the development of inflammatory diseases, which may be the cause of the perinatal death in the knockout mice. 50 , 51 In addition to regulating the occurrence of inflammatory responses, PTPN2 is also involved in bacterial clearance. The targeted removal of PTPN2 within epithelial cells led to the epithelium’s inability to enhance the expression of antimicrobial peptides, which ultimately resulted in an unsuccessful clearance of E. coli infection. 52 PTPN2 expression loss led to autophagy defects and impaired lysosomal acidification, affecting macrophage response to adherent-invasive E. coli . 53 This study examined the impact of SPD on PTPN2 activation in macrophages following MRSA infection. SPD upregulating PTPN2 gene expression and significantly increasing PTPN2 protein levels in macrophages. Critically, the downregulation of PTPN2 expression eliminated the regulation of macrophages by SPD. These results suggested that SPD promoted bacterial clearance by activating PTPN2 expression in macrophages and that PTPN2 activation could also promote the transformation of the M2 phenotype, thereby inhibiting excessive inflammatory responses.

This study is the first to report the protective role of the gut microbiota-associated metabolite spermidine in MRSA bloodstream infection. This protective effect was primarily mediated by up-regulating expression of PTPN2 in macrophages, inhibiting STAT1 phosphorylation, thereby promoting macrophage M2 polarization and suppressing excessive inflammatory responses. However, our focus was solely on the effects of spermidine on macrophages, and we did not investigate its impact on other immune cells. Future studies could employ single-cell sequencing to clarify whether spermidine acts on other immune cells. Additionally, while we knocked down PTPN2 at the cellular level, it is necessary to conduct conditional knockout of PTPN2 at the organism level to further confirm its role. Our study investigates the impact of gut microbiota and its metabolite spermidine on MRSA bloodstream infections, suggesting the broader clinical therapeutic potential of spermidine.
sections.conclusion: In summary, gut microbiota dysbiosis leads to a reduction in spermidine, which is a key process in aggravation of MRSA bloodstream infection. This was confirmed by the fact that oral supplementation with SPD could significantly relieve bloodstream infection. SPD treatment decreased inflammation factor expression by promoting macrophage M2 phenotype polarization. Finally, high PTPN2 expression mediated this effect of SPD. SPD can be used as an adjunctive antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory drug to treat bloodstream infection caused by MRSA, providing new perspectives for the treatment of MRSA infections.
